newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian protests give police the run-around.
newsitem.headline: Serbian protests give police the run-around.

text.p: Non-stop protests by Serbian students stretch into a fifth day on Thursday as Belgrade citizens baffled police with a hide-and-seek strategy to evade a ban on marches.
But the authorities showed no sign of backing off and sowed more confusion to avoid or delay accepting opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition victories at November 17 elections.
Riot police, locked in a standoff with the students in the centre of Belgrade were given the run-around by hundreds of Zajedno supporters.

The protesters' sudden appearances and disappearances in different parts of town kept police racing from district to district to prevent local columns from joining forces for a march into the city centre.
There was no violence. Even the police, in most cases, were in jovial mood.

Belgrade's election commissioners, whose earlier ruling that the opposition won control of local government in the capital is being challenged in court, handed down their decisions on nine more city assembly seats.
Four went to the ruling leftist alliance, four to Zajedno and one to the Radical Party. One seat remains, pending a ruling by a municipal court.

The commission, dominated by the ruling Socialist Party, reinstated Zajedno's nullified victory in the capital last week but the Socialists and their allies in neocommunist Yugoslav United Left appealed to the Supreme Court.
"It is a world champion-class legalistic mess, meticulously crafted to exhaust just about everyone -- Zajedno, the students and the West. Sorry, it won't work," a western diplomat said.

The students showed no sign of tiring. Thousands of them continued their non-stop protests in front of a police cordon in Belgrade centre for the fifth day, vowing not to budge until they are allowed to walk around the city again.
They were joined later in the evening by five former police inspectors who handed out booklets to their former colleagues.
Four student leaders lobbying for support in Washington met U.S. Assistant Secretary of State John Kornblum in his office on Wednesday, the State Department announced.
The students told Kornblum they were afraid the Serbian authorities, who have been relatively restrained so far in their handling of the protests, might soon resort to violence.

"They said that they believed that their country was now at a crossroads and that there was a danger of yet another war in Yugoslavia -- this would be a civil war inside Serbia -- or there was the possibility of a democratic development," Kornblum said.

The United States, which has demanded that Milosevic accept the election results and hand over control of city assemblies, is imposing new sanctions on Belgrade including witholding high-level visits and discouraging trade.
Daily demonstrations by students and Zajedno demanding the government reinstate opposition victories in 14 cities, including Belgrade, are in their 10th week.
President Slobodan Milosevic, facing the most serious challenge of his 10-year rule, has so far refused to accept the opposition triumphs, despite immense pressure by the West.

The student rally swelled to about 30,000 people on Wednesday. Many citizens brought food and drinks and women students kissed policemen and professors, who have sided with the students, challenged the police to a football match.

Zajedno supporters rallied at a nearby square for an afternoon demonstration on the 66th day of protests across Serbia. Zajedno again placed large red screen in front of the police cordon to hide it from view.
